claims.claim_text: The free-market and deregulation-oriented economic doctrine criticized by the DSA holds that economic growth requires eliminating environmental and occupational health and safety regulations together with weakening legal guarantees of workers' union-organizing rights.
The free-market economic doctrine criticized by the DSA treats government provision as inherently inferior to private goods.
The U.S. private health-insurance system fails to meet the needs of millions of people.

The DSA characterizes conservative U.S. policy as deliberately underfunding public provision by shifting the tax burden from corporations and wealthy people to middle- and low-income communities, in order to make public provision fail.

The DSA attributes deterioration in ordinary Americans' living standards during the three decades preceding its 2007 economic-justice statement to government redistribution of income, wealth and power upward combined with corporate victories over unions.

The DSA attributes developing countries' indebtedness and impoverishment to Washington Consensus free-trade policies lacking international guarantees of human, environmental and labor rights, together with IMF and World Bank structural-adjustment programs.

The DSA characterizes Washington Consensus policies as enabling global corporate elites to search internationally for production sites with the cheapest and most vulnerable labor, driving downward competition in labor conditions.
In the DSA's 2007 account, global corporations can locate operations in weak states unable or unwilling to enforce human rights, labor standards or environmental regulations.
The DSA characterizes global corporate elites as exploiting labor worldwide and causing environmental harm.
